line: Hi, I'm Ruth Hale. I run the adult programs here at the library. Are you finding everything okay?
Welcome. The printer's by the desk, the quiet room's upstairs, and the good chairs are gone by ten. Are you new to the neighbourhood?
Then I'll do my speech. It's short. English classes Monday and Wednesday, citizenship class Tuesdays, and a potluck on Thursday nights that's mostly an excuse to meet people.
No, of course. Most people who come on Thursdays don't take any class. A lot of them just want to meet someone who isn't from their own street.
Whoever shows up. Last month a retired judge and a woman who came over in 1998 found out they'd lived on the same block in Queens, years apart. They talked until I turned the lights off.
Whatever they cook at home. That's the only rule. One man brought store cookies for three months, and then one week a pot of something his mother used to make. He stood next to it the whole night.
It was gone by seven. He's brought it every week since. $ I don't need anybody to stop cooking what they cook. I just need them in the same room on a Thursday.
Before this I taught English in Queens for nine years. The first week, people always sat with whoever spoke their language. By the tenth week they didn't. I liked the tenth week.
choice2: Nine years. That's a lot of classes.

line: Sometimes. Some people go to their own center and their own church and come here only for forms, and that's fine. $ What I don't want is two neighbourhoods on one street that never meet. Some days it feels like that's what we've got.
choice1: It doesn't have to stay that way.

line: Hi. Sorry, I'm in your way. I'm Ruth Hale, from the Elm Street Library. I'm leaving flyers, and the clinic gives me one corner of one table.
choice1: Hi, I'm {playerName}. What are the flyers for?

line: Ninety-one in May. He's been here since the sixties and never took the test. He says he wants to vote once before he goes. He sits in the front row and corrects my dates.
His granddaughter registered to vote, and he went along to watch. He told me he stood outside the booth like a man outside a church. $ The next Tuesday he was in Room 3 with a notebook.
Please. Put one by the mailboxes, not on the door, people pull them off doors. I print them in four languages. I honestly don't know if anyone reads those.

line: That's what {homeLeader} told me. Big date, big time, and say there's food. I keep trying to get {homeCenter} to co-host something with us in the spring. Do you know her?

Because people go where they already go. If it's at the library, half of them won't come. If it's at {homeCenter}, half of ours won't. With both names on the flyer, maybe everybody comes and nobody's the guest.

line: Every week. Somebody also drew a moustache on the eagle. The front desk says it was a kid. I think it's the man in the blue jacket who waits for his insulin on Tuesdays.
No. He's here every Tuesday, at the same time as my class, and he's never once come. Maybe the moustache is a start. _straightens the pile_ I'll leave one on his chair.
Ruth is taping a new potluck sign-up sheet to the end of the desk. "Somebody signed the last one 'Biscuit.' That's the lost cat on the board. Either it's a joke or the cat is coming Thursday."
Not yet. The owner checks the board every morning on her way to work, and now so do I. $ That's what a board is for, honestly. Half the people who come in here only come to read it.

line: Morning, {playerName}. Do you have a second? I'm trying to get {homeCenter} to co-host something in the spring.
A health fair, maybe. Blood pressure at one table, benefits sign-up at the next, library cards at the door. Do you know {homeLeader} over there?
choice1: Who else do you need on board?

line: Frank DeLuca, for the Fifth Street end. He'll tell me it's not his kind of thing and then send six folding tables. $ People here come when I ask, mostly because I never stop asking. Frank comes when his customers do. Do you know {homeLeader}?
Morning, {playerName}. Do you have a second? I need four signatures from Fifth Street for the block-party potluck, and every one of them will ask Frank first.
Frank DeLuca, the hardware store. On Fifth nothing gets signed until Frank has nodded at it. He's not against a potluck. He just doesn't come to them, and he wonders out loud who they're for.

Work around him, honestly. His wife reads my flyers, and the diner owes me for tax night. $ [neutral] And I'll ask {homeLeader} to put {homeCenter}'s name on it beside ours. Then Fifth isn't the host, it's a guest, and guests don't need Frank's nod.
Yes. Walk down Fifth with me on Saturday with a clipboard. They say no to me on the phone. They say yes to two people standing in the doorway, especially when one of them can say it in two languages.
Oh, good, it's you. Can I ask you an honest question?
When we print the flyers in other languages, does anyone read them? Or do they just make us feel good about ourselves?
choice1: People read them. Put the date in big numbers.
choice2: Ask the people you want to come.

line: Big numbers. Okay. Fourteen years at this and I still get it wrong. Last fall I put 'all welcome' in four languages on a flyer for a church basement, and then wondered why half the neighbourhood stayed home.
It was a church that wasn't theirs. I thought an open door was the same as people feeling welcome to walk through it. $ [warm] Now I go and ask first. It takes longer. It's usually worth it.
Thursday's potluck: three new families are coming for the first time, and I'd like you at their table. You know what it's like to be new here. Will you come?
Nothing special. Sit with them, pass the food, tell them where the good printer is. The first night is the hard one. After that people come back for each other, not for me.
You seem to know people here and at {homeCenter}. Come to Thursday's potluck? I'd like you at the table with the new families.
Because you can sit between the two tables and not belong to one more than the other. Or to both, I'm not sure how you'd put it. Most people can't do that yet.
Hi. Sorry, I'm counting chairs. I put out twenty for the citizenship class, and I think I need ten.
Hi. Sorry, I'm counting flyers. I used to leave twenty here every week for the citizenship class. I think this week I need ten.
Half. Since the speech. People won't write their address on a sign-up sheet anymore. I don't blame them.

choice3: That's hard. I'll let you get on.

line: I took the address line off on Tuesday. First names only now. The county wants numbers for the grant, so I count heads, and that's it.
I thought about it. {homeLeader} offered a room at {homeCenter}. Some people would come there who won't come to the library, and the other way round. Maybe we do both nights.

Some. The man who's ninety came. He said he was here before any of them were born and he isn't going to start hiding now. $ Two of the young mothers didn't. I called. They were very polite, and they didn't come.
Hi. You caught me in a good mood. I just got an email I've been waiting six years for.

line: The federal grant came through. Two more English sections, and money for phone interpreters on citizenship nights. I've asked for that line in the budget for six years.

line: Hi. Sorry, I'm making a list of everyone who knows a lawyer. It's a short list.

line: Because the library is where she reads her letters. $ I'll say it plainly, since nobody on the council will: this policy is wrong.
